articles.title: Watch: BBC reports from the front-line of an escalating war in Yemen
articles.summary: In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone the BBC travels to the front line with pro-government soldiers.

blocks.text: In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone, the BBC has travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where the Houthi control ends and no man's land begins.

Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war.
From the front-line a drone is heard above, which a soldier accompanying the crew in south-western Yemen said is usually followed by an attack.
Within about 10 minutes, after the crew had driven away, the loud thuds of strikes followed, senior international investigations correspondent Nawal Al-Maghafi reports.

articles.title: Blanche defends Trump’s White House media ban: ‘It’s a privilege … not a right’
articles.summary:
US attorney general argues that president is ‘sick and tired’ of inaccurate reporting by CNN, MS Now and Politico

Donald Trump’s…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s attorney general Todd Blanche argued on Sunday that the administration banned three news outlets from the White House because it is “privilege … not a right” to be there.

Appearing on the ABC News program This Week during the second week of the White House’s dispute over press credentialing and access, Blanche also said that the administration took the decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico beginning on 19 September because the president was “sick and tired” of what he considered to be those media outlets’ inaccurate reporting.

On Thursday, a judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the credentials of affected journalists, and they were allowed entry to the executive complex.
But on Saturday, CNN said its journalists were barred from joining the press pool traveling with the president on Air Force One.

“The president hasn’t denied access,” Blanche told the outlet. “That’s not the right way to describe it.” He pointed to Trump’s comments that he is “sick and tired” of certain media outlets’ reporting that the president considers inaccurate.
“There’s still obviously litigation going on, but the important thing … is to know that … being in the White House is a privilege. It’s not a right,” Blanche said.

The continuing dispute between the administration and the White House press corp had appeared to be resolving before CNN was again blocked for pool coverage. That was after outlets stood in solidarity with CNN, MS Now and Politico by briefly refusing to carry pool TV feeds of the president.
On ABC, Blanche said it wasn’t unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed on to the president’s plane.
“The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One,” Blanche said. “This wasn’t a one-time denial of CNN. There’s all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying.
“It’s not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it’s common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president.”
Blanche repeated the administration’s position that the affected three outlets’ reporting amounted to a “national security problem”.

Trump has said that there was not any “particular reason” for the action against CNN, MS Now and Politico, arguing “they purposely write negative news, and they do that because they want to … diminished the Republicans and a Republican administration”.

In the ruling to temporarily restore the three banned outlets’ White House access for 14 days, US district judge Timothy Kelly said there was nothing in the record suggesting that revocation of the press passes was motivated by national security concerns.

“Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the White House – instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote in his ruling.

Trump was faced with a gloomy political landscape with just over a month before the federal midterm elections in November. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s overall public approval rating to be at 32%, an all-time low.

But confidence in the news media polls lower, with just 28% expressing a “great deal” or “fair amount” of trust in newspapers, television channels and radio outlets to report the news fully, accurately and fairly, according to a 2025 Gallup survey.

Bill Clinton recently commented on the battle between what the news media see as a crude effort at censorship and a denial of constitutional rights – and what the White House views as unfairly negative reporting.

“There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps,” the former president said at the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 summit. “And there’s a reason we have a constitution – because none of us are immune from being pissed off.
“But I’m glad I never did, and I’m glad I couldn’t. And these people shouldn’t. The law should be what it is.”
Blanche was asked what the US constitution’s first amendment – which guarantees the right to a free press – meant to him.

“The law says – what the free press can do is they are free to report whatever they want,” Blanche remarked. “Of course, they can. But when it comes to the White House, it is the people’s house. It is a privilege and not a right to be there.”
He added that “it is absolutely the president’s duty to make sure that the American people are hearing accurate news.”

articles.title: Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections
articles.summary: Aleksandar Vučić's administration has been dogged by prolonged protests over allegations of corruption.

blocks.text: Serbia's president has resigned after more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption.
Aleksandar Vučić said his administration had preserved peace and stability during his nine-year tenure as he addressed supporters outside the presidential building in the capital, Belgrade.

He had already announced his intention to resign in June and is currently standing to be his party's candidate for prime minister in the upcoming parliamentary elections. Vučić cannot run for a third presidential term under Serbia's constitution.
The pro-Russian populist's administration has been dogged by anger over alleged corner-cutting.
It was the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station's roof, killing 16 people, that first galvanised anger towards the government in 2024.
Protests involving a wide range of citizens - from students and teachers to workers and farmers - followed.

Demonstrators believed that the disaster reflected more than a decade of governing by the Progressive Party of Vucic, who closely associated himself with the station's renovation, which was supposed to be a symbol of Serbia's progress.

A series of resignations of those under the embattled president failed to placate the protesters, who continued to demonstrate throughout this summer, turning to unrest following accusations of police brutality.
Vučić's presidency was due to expire next year. Under Serbia's constitution, presidential elections must be held no more than three months after his resignation.
This means Serbians will go to the polls twice before the end of the year.

Vučić said the presidential election will take place more than a month after the snap parliamentary election in late October, itself called in response to the protests, which had added calls for a vote to their list of demands.
He had earlier announced that he planned to run in that election as Progressive Party's leader, leaving the possibility he could retain a position at the top of Serbian politics.
Parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabić, also a Progressive Party member, will assume the role of interim president until a new one is elected.

Vučić used his constitutional powers to pardon 49 people, including 23 students and party loyalists suspected of offences related to what he called the "terrible events we have gone through over the past year and a half", according to Serbian public broadcaster RTS.

The upcoming parliamentary elections will pit Vučić's Progressive Party against a student-led, anti-corruption movement called Students Win and a coalition of pro-Western opposition parties known as European Serbia.
Vucic has been a fixture of Serbian politics for more than a decade, becoming prime minister in 2014, before being elected to his first term as president in 2017.
He has publicly said he wants Serbia to join the EU while courting close ties with Russia and opening Serbia up to Chinese investment.

articles.title: Republican senator criticizes White House for taxpayer-funded Trump ads
articles.summary:
John Kennedy pushes back against such spending as pro-Trump ‘public service announcements’ air before midterms

As the White House expands a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promote

blocks.text: As the White House expands a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promote Donald Trump’s political agenda before the November midterm elections, US senator John Kennedy told CBS News on Sunday “there ought to be a rule” against such spending – before tacitly admitting such spending is “probably” illegal.

Kennedy, the US president’s fellow Republican, was asked by Margaret Brennan, the CBS Face the Nation host, about the White House spending to air multiple ads featuring Trump – including one that was produced for his 2024 election campaign.

Brennan first reminded Kennedy that in March he had rebuked Kristi Noem, then Trump’s homeland security secretary, for spending millions in government funds “to bolster her public image” in a $220m series of ads she starred in. She then asked the Louisiana senator to comment on the new ads featuring Trump, which the White House calls “public service announcements”.

“Our viewers are going to see a 30-second commercial on this program,” Brennan said. “It’s on all major networks – it’s on the cable networks as well. It prominently features President Trump, and there’s a voice praising him as ‘the toughest, most resilient person I ever met’. And at the end, it says ‘paid for by the US government’. Is that the best use of taxpayer money?”
Kennedy replied: “Well, first, as to secretary Noem, what she did was masterclass dumb. She spent $220[m] on commercials about her, and I called her out on it.”

“This looks like a commercial about President Trump,” Brennan noted, referring to the first ad in the series, a 30-second highlight reel of Trump’s second presidency, punctuated by on-screen text driving his political agenda and suggesting Democrats are communists.

“I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money … on private ads for themselves,” Kennedy replied. “Now, the White House sees it differently. But … I think there ought to be a rule that you can’t – well, there probably is a rule – you can’t spend public money to promote yourself.”

Kennedy, a lawyer with degrees from both the University of Virginia and University of Oxford, appeared to be tacitly acknowledging the argument made by Jamie Raskin, a Democratic congressman and legal scholar, that any government employees who worked on the first pro-Trump ad – “or used government resources to make it” – may have committed a felony violation of the Hatch act, a law that bars government workers from partisan campaign activities.

According to Medium Buying, a company that buys airtime for Republican candidates, the Trump administration used more taxpayer funds to broadcast another partisan ad featuring the president that aired nationwide on Saturday during a college football game between Ohio State and Illinois on Fox. It aired again during Fox News Sunday.
That 30-second spot shows a moody, black-and-white shot of Trump staring into the camera as the soundtrack plays the closing riff of a campaign speech he gave dozens of times in 2023 and 2024.

“This is the final battle,” Trump says in the ad. “With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state; we will expel the warmongers from our government; we will drive out the globalists; we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,” he continues, with cheers from a crowd. Those cheers indicate that the audio was recorded during a campaign rally and at a time before he used his power as president to start a war with Iran that has left some supporters feeling betrayed.

“We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate our country from these tyrants and villains once and for all,” Trump can be heard promising in language clearly calculated to appeal to Christian supporters by echoing the biblical story of Jesus driving merchants and money changers from the temple in Jerusalem.
after newsletter promotion

The newest ad, with on-screen text reading “Paid for by the US Government”, is even more obviously a partisan product than the first one. In fact, the ad was created for Trump’s 2024 election campaign. And it was posted on his Truth Social account in 2023 and 2024 with a plea for funds from supporters.

blocks.caption: A screenshot from a Trump campaign ad played at the Republican national convention on 18 July 2024. Photograph: CSPAN

blocks.text: The ad was even played on giant screens during the 2024 Republican national convention before Trump’s speech accepting his party’s nomination. When it was broadcast during the convention by C-SPAN on 18 July 2024, the ad was identified as material “provided by the Republican National Committee”.
At the end of his interview with CBS on Sunday, Kennedy volunteered that he also opposed Trump’s drive to put his own name on public buildings.
“I also think that we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him while he’s alive,” Kennedy said, before adding that there is such a statute in his home state.

“Well, we’ll watch, Senator, if you introduce that,” Brennan responded, reminding the Republican lawmaker that making statements on Sunday morning television shows is not the same as using his power to actually introduce legislation that could restrain Trump.

articles.title: Bill Gates joins call for AI safeguards, wants to discuss concerns with Trump
articles.summary: AI requires safeguards that go beyond self-regulation, ‌Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said in an interview that aired on Sunday, calling for legislation to be passed in Congress. A groundswell has…

image.caption: Bill Gates is calling for AI legislation, joining a growing number of tech giants. (Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

AI requires safeguards that go beyond self-regulation, ‌Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said in an interview that aired on Sunday, calling for legislation to be passed in Congress. A groundswell has ​risen in favour of federal intervention after OpenAI said in July an autonomous AI agent went rogue during a security test and hacked into another company
'No one thinks self-regulation is enough,' the Microsoft co-founder told NBC
AI requires safeguards that go beyond self-regulation, ‌Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said in an interview that aired on Sunday, calling for legislation to be passed in Congress.

"You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like," Gates said in a taped interview on NBC's Meet the Press program. "And that ​has to be a required thing."

A sudden groundswell has ​risen in favour of federal intervention after OpenAI said in July that an autonomous AI agent went rogue during a security test and hacked into another company, subverting human control. Gates ​joined that chorus, saying government must be involved.
"No one thinks self-regulation is enough," he ⁠said.
In a rare show ⁠of unity, the CEOs of rivals Anthropic, OpenAI, Google's DeepMind, ‌Microsoft and xAI have called for slowing the development of increasingly capable AI systems.
Bill Gates warns unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’

OpenAI said Friday it had paused training of its latest AI models, just hours after the company disclosed it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching U.S. federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.
Separately, AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a U.S. Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.
'It's not a hoax at all'

But U.S. President Donald Trump and other opponents of additional regulation for AI say new government restrictions would simply give China the upper hand in the AI revolution. Trump has publicly dismissed calls for new laws on ⁠AI as a "hoax."
Gates argued that safeguards would not dramatically hinder the industry, and that the risks of not implementing them are real.
"It's not a hoax at all," he told NBC.
Gates has said he wants to meet Trump to ‌discuss AI.
"I hope that, given my life's work in the field, my saying how unique and different this is and how concerned I am will add to what he's hearing from other people," Gates said.

items: OpenAI pauses training of latest models after AI agents probed U.S. government sites in unexpected ways
AI's 'warning shot': Tech companies, experts raise fears of more rogue swarms after alarming Hugging Face hack

blocks.text: Axios reported that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei will have dinner on Sunday with Trump at ​the White House. Anthropic and the White House did not immediately return a request for comment on the Axios report.
Warnings about AI's risks are not ⁠new. But they took on added urgency this month after researchers in leading AI labs attached both a timeline ⁠and a probability to those concerns.
We've been warned about AI — but could it actually kill humanity? | About That

Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned that AI could kill us all by ⁠the ⁠end of the decade, prompting U.S. lawmakers to ​call for new rules to govern the technology. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's alignment science lead, echoed Coxon's warning, saying there was ​a more than 10 per cent chance ⁠of such an event within the next decade.

Some policymakers have proposed mandating a "kill switch" that would allow federal authorities to halt AI models. Gates said that while he was not opposed to some sort of kill switch, it would not be enough if other safeguards were not also implemented.
The U.S. and China agreed to launch a dialogue on AI following President Xi ⁠Jinping's recent visit to Washington.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announces resignation
articles.summary: Aleksandar Vucic will now be running to be prime minister in the upcoming snap elections slated for next month.

image.caption: Vucic was serving his second term and would have left office in May of 2027Image: Ludovic Marin/AFP

blocks.text: Serbia's long-time President Aleksandar Vucic announced on Sunday that he would resign from his post in order to run for prime minister in the upcoming October snap elections.
From the presidential palace in Belgrade, Vucic spoke to supporters: "I am resigning as president."
"Tomorrow morning I will hand over my duties to the parliament speaker," he added
Vucic is banned by the Serbian Constitution from seeking a third term. He was serving his second term and would have left office in May of 2027.
This is a developing story, more details to come...

articles.title: Serbia’s populist president Aleksandar Vučić resigns to run for prime minister
articles.summary:
Vučić not allowed to seek third presidential term and PM election will test his grip on rule after widespread protests

Serbia’s populist president, Aleksandar Vučić, has resigned to pursue…

blocks.text: Serbia’s populist president, Aleksandar Vučić, has resigned to pursue an attempt to become the prime minister in an upcoming early parliamentary election that will test his firm rule in the Balkan country after nearly two years of protests.

Vučić’s second presidential term would otherwise end in May next year. He is banned by the Serbian constitution from seeking a third term and said he was resigning to lead his rightwing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) in the 25 October ballot.

The governing populists face a major challenge at the ballot from a youth-backed movement that led the protests triggered by a train station canopy collapse in November 2024 that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad.

University students demanded accountability for the tragedy. Their struggle for justice and against corruption has grown into a strong movement that will attempt to oust Vučić’s government after 14 years in power. Vučić has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years.
“I am resigning the duty of the president of the republic,” Vučić said, reading the text of his resignation.

The ballot in October will be held against a backdrop of high political tensions as Vučić’s populists seek to remain in office despite widespread discontent. His decision to run for prime minister is seen both as an attempt to retain a top position, and to boost his party’s chances against the student movement.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Vučić light flares outside the presidency of Serbia in Belgrade after his resignation. Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/Reuters

blocks.text: In recent weeks Vučić has toured the country with live coverage on pro-government media. He has opened new roads, offered assistance money and cheaper medicines, and visited voters in their homes. More recently, he was filmed driving in his brother’s car to some of the events.

The prime minister in Serbia is formally more powerful than the president. But Vučić still took a dominant role during his two five-year terms, sometimes presiding over government sessions and routinely announcing all important decisions and plans.

Serbia’s independent Bureau for Social Research has filed a complaint alleging that Vučić has abused a public institution as president to promote his party, which he has dismissed. There has been no response from the anti-corruption authorities that are under government control.

After Vučić’s resignation, the acting president will be a close ally and former prime minister, Ana Brnabić, who is the outgoing speaker of Serbia’s 250-member parliament. After a new parliament is elected in the 25 October ballot, the new speaker will take over from Brnabić, appoint the prime minister and schedule a presidential vote.

Vučić and his party have been accused of rampant corruption, organised crime links and a clampdown on democratic freedoms, including the critical media. The SNS have gradually taken control of all state institutions since coming to power in 2012, while denying abuse of office and repeatedly pledging to fight graft.

The student-backed election list includes little-known experts, professors, teachers, athletes and other individuals from all walks of life. Groups of students have been touring the country on bicycles as part of their campaign urging the rule of law and an end to corruption.

Analysts say the student group and Vučić are polling closely, heralding a tight race and a referendum-like atmosphere. Also running are Vučić’s allies, the Socialist party, a pro-EU opposition alliance and several smaller groups.

Authorities have pushed hard against protesters with police violence and detentions, as Vučić, without offering evidence, accused his opponents and critical media of an intention to “destroy the state” under unspecified foreign influence.
He told Serbia’s state RTS Television earlier on Sunday that foreign powers and unidentified people in the country planned to stir unrest on election night.
Serbia’s efforts to join the EU have stalled under Vučić because of democratic backsliding and a refusal to join sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Tragically Hip, Feist and more inducted into Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame
articles.summary: The memory of the late Gord Downie was in sharp focus as the Kingston alt-rock band the Tragically Hip were among four musical acts inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame at a…

image.caption: From left: Paul Langlois, Rob Baker and Gord Sinclair of the Tragically Hip speak after being inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame on stage in Toronto Saturday. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment

The memory of the late Gord Downie was in sharp focus as the Kingston alt-rock band the Tragically Hip were among four musical acts inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame at a star-studded gala held at Toronto's Massey Hall on Saturday night.
Roch Voisine and members of Loverboy also inducted in Toronto ceremony Saturday
As members of the Tragically Hip took the stage to accept the honour, the band paid tribute to their bandmate, who died in 2017 after he was diagnosed with a rare and incurable form of brain cancer.
Guitarist Rob Baker shared a message he said was from Downie, "who couldn't be here."

"I stood before the songwriters' cabal, bearing gifts of drugs and alcohol. That's not enough, and that's not all. Wait over there until your number's called. I stood before the songwriters' cabal, all wide-eyed and enthralled, just to be included at all," said Baker, who stood on stage alongside his bandmates Gord Sinclair and Paul Langlois.
The Hip entered the 2026 class along with Toronto indie music pioneer Feist, the songwriting duo behind rock band Loverboy (Mike Reno and Paul Dean) and French-Canadian artist Roch Voisine.

items: Tragically Hip band members reflect on Gord Downie and farewell tour 10 years after final show
Celebratory crowd gathers in Kingston, Ont., to watch Tragically Hip's final concert

blocks.text: The inductees' beloved songs provided the soundtrack for the evening that had the crowd tapping their feet, clapping their hands and dancing in their seats as performers, including Finneas, Our Lady Peace, Wilco's Jeff Tweedy and others who took the stage for the genre-spanning tributes that covered arena rock to indie pop to love ballads.

As the tribute to the Hip closed out the night's ceremonies, a purple feathered hat hung on a microphone stand on stage, a nod to Downie's eclectic fashion. Allison Russell, who was among the artists performing the Hip's music, blew a kiss to the mic stand as she began Wheat Kings, then ended the song by saying, "We will always love you, Gord."

items: Angine de Poitrine were the big winners at this year's Polaris Music Prize gala
Canadian Country Music Awards take over SaskTel Centre in Saskatoon

blocks.text: Baker said in his speech that the band had been thrilled "to have such a great frontman."

"I remember taking (bassist) Gord Sinclair down to see him at a place in Kingston, saying, 'You've got to see this guy, we're going to stand on his coattails and ride them,"' said Baker in his speech, which also noted the Hip's practice of sharing songwriting credit among all the band members.
Finneas performs, inducts Feist

Earlier in the evening, the Los Angeles songwriter and producer Finneas inducted Leslie Feist. The brother of Billie Eilish told a charming story about a chance meeting with the Toronto singer-songwriter at an airport in 2018 before calling her an "incredibly important, inspiring figure in my life." Finneas performed her 2007 song My Moon My Man.

As she accepted her accolade on stage, Feist told the crowd, "talking is harder than singing for me" before launching into a speech that detailed how the 50-year-old musician used songs to process the ebbs and flows of her life.

"If all of the messy and meaningful and honest work can eventually lead anyone to a moment like this, then that's how I figured out how to stand here and genuinely from my heart say thank you," said Feist, who received video messages from notable figures such as Sam Smith, Joe Jonas, Olivia Rodrigo and director Jacob Tierney, whose hit TV show Heated Rivalry featured two Feist songs.

Among the evening's many captivating performances was Tweedy, who host George Stroumboulopoulos introduced as one of the best living songwriters. The Wilco frontman sang a heartfelt cover of Feist's mournful song The Park.
Lots of love for Loverboy

Earlier, Canadian songstress Amanda Marshall opened the show with a booming rendition of Loverboy's 1980 hit Turn Me Loose that had the audience up from their seats immediately, while Toronto folk singer Charlotte Cornfield followed with a smooth and soulful performance of Feist's How Come You Never Go There.

Later, the Ottawa-based musician Talk, wearing a fitted baby blue jumpsuit with fringed sleeves, rocked the venue with a high-energy cover of Loverboy's classic hit Working for the Weekend, earning him a standing ovation.

The night also included notes of Canadian pride. Jim Vallance, inducted into the Hall of Fame alongside songwriting partner Bryan Adams in 2022, began his tribute to Loverboy by saying he was "so proud to be Canadian" and pointed out that the nation punched above its weight in producing great musicians.

Dean, Loverboy's guitarist, accepted the honour on behalf of himself and lead singer Reno, who could not attend. Dean also thanked the other members of the band, including former bassist Scott Smith, who died in 2000 following a boating accident.
Voisine performs emotional duet
Other highlights included Olympic hockey gold medallists Laura Stacey and Marie Philip-Poulin, who inducted Voisine and noted the 63-year-old's time playing hockey before he took up music.

Voisine said in his speech he started writing songs only for himself. But while studying at the University of Ottawa, he'd practice his songs in his residence's stairwell and later learned fellow students would study along with his music.

Following his bilingual speech, in which he thanked his family and songwriting collaborators, Voisine performed an emotional, choir-backed duet of his ballad I'll Always Be There with French Canadian artist Isabelle Boulay.
Beloved Canadian alt-rock band Our Lady Peace closed out the show with a high-octane cover of the Hip's Locked in the Trunk of a Car.
Lead singer Raine Maida shared how watching a performance by the Tragically Hip when he was 18 inspired him to chase art over entertainment.
Before beginning the song, he told the crowd to get on their feet.
"And light your phones up for Mr. Gord Downie."

articles.title: Republican says Trump’s support of Ken Paxton in Texas primary was ‘colossal mistake’
articles.summary:
Thom Tillis says Trump’s decision to back Paxton over John Cornyn has put the Senate seat at risk for Republicans

US senator Thom Tillis on Sunday criticized

blocks.text: US senator Thom Tillis on Sunday criticized Donald Trump, his fellow Republican, for the president’s support of Ken Paxton over incumbent John Cornyn in the Texas Senate Republican primary.

“He made a colossal mistake,” Tillis, a frequent Trump critic from North Carolina, said during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union in reference to the president’s support of Paxton who defeated Cornyn in the May primary.
“John Cornyn’s a great member of the US Senate. Paxton has his challenges,” the retiring Tillis added. “We would not be spending tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in Texas if Cornyn had won.”
Tillis pointed to the president’s involvement in the contest and described Trump’s decision to back Paxton instead of Cornyn as an “unforced error” that has put the Senate seat at risk for the GOP.

Trump endorsed Paxton just days before the Texas attorney general defeated Cornyn, a four-term senator, and advanced to face Democratic candidate James Talarico, a in the general election on 3 November.

The race had wide implications for Trump’s strength heading into November’s midterm federal elections. Paxton will now face Talarico, a Democratic pastor and state legislator whose message of peace and populism has attracted much attention. If he wins, Talarico would become the first Democrat in more than 30 years to win statewide office in Texas.
When he chose to support Paxton over Cornyn, Trump highlighted the Texas attorney general’s record as a steadfast supporter of the president’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement.
Cornyn had previously said during the 2024 presidential campaign that Republicans should move on from Trump.
In a social media post shortly before the election day, Trump said Cornyn had been “VERY disloyal” to him and implored voters in Texas to “REMEMBER!”

Paxton, meanwhile, is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption and later acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate. He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud, but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pretrial diversion agreement.
In July 2025, his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce “on biblical grounds”, citing adultery.

Tillis is one of a handful of Republicans to repeatedly break with Trump and publicly criticize the president’s decisions. In April, he spoke out in defense of the Nato military alliance after Trump said he was “absolutely” considering withdrawing the US from it.

“Any president that contemplates attempting to withdraw from Nato is not only fulfilling [Russian leader] Vladimir Putin and [Chinese premier] Xi Jinping’s greatest dreams but would be undermining America’s own national security interests,” Tillis said at the time.

He also called for then secretary of homeland security Kristi Noem’s resignation after immigration agents killed two US citizens in Minneapolis in January, calling her leadership “a disaster” during the last Senate hearing before her firing.

Tillis was one of a small number of Republicans on Thursday to vote in favor of a Democrat-led war powers resolution that aimed to end the US war with Iran. Despite gaining some Republican support, the proposal failed to pass in the Senate by a 49-50 vote.

articles.title: Yemen: Houthis report deadly Saudi strikes on Taiz market
articles.summary: The Houthi-run health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," vowing to retaliate. The Houthis' account of the attack cannot be independently verified.

image.caption: Children were among those reportedly killed in two Saudi airstrikesImage: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday accused the Saudi Arabian Air Force of having struck a shopping area around the central market of Taiz. The Iran-aligned Houthis said at least seven people had been killed and dozens injured.
What do we know so far?

The group's Al-Masirah TV channel showed footage of large plumes of smoke and a destroyed warehouse stacked with food in cardboard boxes. Al-Masirah TV also reported that children were among those wounded, citing the Houthis' health ministry.

Taiz is currently under the control of Yemeni government forces, but it has long been besieged by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in the country's civil war. Taiz is located in southwestern Yemen.
The escalation in fighting comes after a fragile truce between Yemeni government forces and Houthi rebels broke down months ago and new regional tensions sparked by the Iran war.
The Houthi health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," saying it was directly and deliberately targeting civilian sites in Taiz.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of launching two air raids that hit the market, adding that blood was "unjustly and aggressively spilled" in a statement posted online.
The group has vowed to retaliate.
The claims made by the Houthis cannot be independently verified.
In response to the Houthi report, troops loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen confirmed that their air force had struck a Houthi depot and vehicles in the area.
France sends troops as Houthi attacks threaten Saudi oil
Saudi-backed coalition ramps up attacks after new Houthi offensive
The civil war in Yemen began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government. They went on to take control of vast swaths of the country's north.

Saudi Arabia joined forces against the Houthis the following year, leading an international coalition against them. But so far, Yemen's government forces have not been able to effectively repel the latest Houthi offensive.

Fighting has spiked in September as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast. The rebels have also launched a blockade on Saudi energy exports to coincide with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Renewed clashes are is under way in several parts of the country, with at least 125,000 people displaced by it.
The Yemeni government has meanwhile called for a general mobilization, urging Yemenis to join the army and security forces.
Yemen is one of the poorest in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.
Houthi gains in Yemen threaten key Red Sea shipping route

articles.title: Avalanche in Nepal leaves 2 dead, several missing
articles.summary: An avalanche has struck the Himlung Himal base camp in Nepal after days of severe weather. Two guides are confirmed dead and at least 14 people remain missing in the remote region.

image.caption: The Himalayas in Nepal are home to many peaks popular with tourist climbers from around the globe [FILE: April 17, 2026]Image: Elisa Schu/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two people have died when an avalanche struck the base camp of a mountain in Nepal with at least 14 others still missing.
The avalanche hit the 7,126-meter (23,380-foot) Himlung Himal after several days of heavy rain and snowfall across the region.
The dead and missing are all mountain guides and staff of Nepalese expedition companies who had been preparing the base camp for paying customers to climb the mountain.

"There were a total of 14 kitchen staff members and two climbing guides from different companies who were missing," the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association said. "The two climbing guides have been found, but sadly, both were found deceased."
Unclear how many are missing

There was conflicting information as to how many people were in the affected area near the border with Tibet at the time of disaster. Local police said there were at least 22 people at the base camp when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning.

Bibhuti Chand Thakur, head of trekking company Himalayan Holidays Nepal, told news agency DPA that search and rescue operations were under way. "The chance of survival remains high because of fresh snow," he said, adding that he did not yet have a definitive number of missing or survivors, as the area is remote and cut off from communication.

blocks.caption: While Mount Everest (pictured) is Nepal's most famous peak, peaks like Himlung Himal are also popular with climbers [FILE: May 21, 2024]Image: Narendra Shahi Thakuri/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Authorities had warned of severe weather across Nepal over the weekend. Rain has affected much of the country since Thursday, with snowfall reported in the higher northern regions. The conditions have disrupted roads and trekking routes and led authorities to suspend climbing and trekking activities on several mountains.
The Himalayan nation is home to eight of the world's 14 mountains higher than 8,000 meters, and trekking and mountaineering tourism is vital to the country's economy.
The latest avalanche comes as Nepal continues to recover from devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing.

articles.title: Woman charged with stealing from patients and staff at hospitals across Ontario
articles.summary: The 34-year-old is under investigation for incidents that began in February 2024 up until as recently as last month.

blocks.text: Police in Ontario, Canada, have charged a woman with 65 offences including fraud and theft for allegedly stealing from patients and staff at several healthcare centres in the province.
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) identified the suspect as Nassim Eronn, 34, from Burlington, a city 56km (34 miles) south of Toronto.
"The investigation was initiated following multiple reports of theft and fraud involving patients and staff members within healthcare facilities," police said in a statement to BBC News.
They say the incidents under investigation began in February 2024 and continued until as recently as last month. The suspect worked at health centres across the province.

The suspect faces charges including 34 counts of fraud under $5,000 (£3,800), 13 counts of theft under $5,000 and seven counts of disobeying a court order, according to police. Other charges include breach of trust and impersonation.
OPP began investigating the woman in May after a report of theft when she worked at Orillia Soldiers' Memorial Hospital, about 130km north of Toronto.
"This investigation was prompted by several complaints of theft and fraud from patients and staff within the hospital," police said at the time.
The investigation was expanded to cover more hospitals where further incidents were uncovered.
"Multiple search warrants were executed where significant amounts of property were seized," police said.

articles.title: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war
articles.summary:
Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’

The Trump…

blocks.text: The Trump administration’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejected Iran’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”.

Echoing comments by Donald Trump on Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks ‌on vessels in the strait of Hormuz.

“They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.”

Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at ⁠the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal ⁠to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said.
Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”.
Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace.
Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”.
Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel.

“Our conditions are clear, ​and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.”
Araghchi also appeared on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, saying his country is prepared to resume fighting with the US but has not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal.
“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” Araghchi said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war.
“At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”

The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said his country was ready for ​talks on its nuclear program and other issues – but would not ​accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will ​defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.
On CNN, Waltz also addressed recent reports that China had assisted Iran in missile targeting of shipping in the strait of Hormuz and on US military bases in the region.

Waltz did not confirm the leaked intelligence assessments but said Trump had raised the issue with China premier Xi Jinping during the latter’s recent state visit to the US capital Washington DC. Trump had also done so “multiple times” previously, including during his visit to China in May, according to Waltz.
“I think we have seen movement in a positive direction,” Waltz said. “President Trump has made it clear it’s unacceptable.”
Waltz pointed to readouts of the high-level meeting that said the US and China had “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”.

“They cannot and should not be tolling, much less attacking, international shipping in an international waterway,” Waltz said. “So I think that was incredibly important to hear from President Xi coming out of the summit.”

Waltz also rejected reporting in the Wall Street Journal that the US would resume bombing Iran after the federal midterm elections in November. He pointed to Trump’s comments that Iran was miscalculating.

“The president is looking to make not just this generation – but the next generation – safer by not allowing what is essentially a terrorist organization in [Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] that is controlling the levers of government and wants to march towards a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. “We’re not going to let the IRGC have a nuclear weapon, much less hold the world hostage with one.”

articles.title: Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality
articles.summary: The initiative would have prevented the nation from imposing sanctions unless approved by the UN.

blocks.text: Voters in Switzerland have overwhelmingly rejected a stricter interpretation of the country's tradition of diplomatic neutrality.
More than 70% of Swiss voters rejected proposals that would have prevented the European nation from imposing sanctions without UN approval, official results showed.
The move would have also prevented Switzerland from pursuing closer ties with the Nato military alliance.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reopened the debate around Switzerland's centuries-old non-alignment.
Moscow openly backed the initiative, which was supported by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) and opposed by the federal government and all other major parties.

Lukas Golder, co-director of research institute Gfs.bern told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that Swiss voters had not rejected embracing its neutrality but that the vote showed Switzerland was in favour of sanctions against Russia.
"People have a clear idea of what Switzerland's neutrality is supposed to achieve," he said.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate that "neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility".
While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference".
He added that Switzerland would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace".
Switzerland was internationally recognised in 1815 when the country was granted "eternal neutrality" at the Congress of Vienna, during a period of war and upheaval in Europe.

This neutrality was legally defined by the Hague Convention of 1907, which forbade Switzerland supplying weapons to countries at war. It previously rejected a request from Germany for ammunition for tanks being sent to Kyiv.
Switzerland remained neutral through World War Two. It also banked gold looted by the Nazis and, in a move designed to keep Nazi Germany from invading, turned away thousands of Jewish refugees.
Switzerland apologised for the policies in the 1990s.
Switzerland's system of direct democracy means major political decisions are often deferred to the voters through referenda.

articles.title: Nor’easter storm batters US east coast with heavy winds and power outages
articles.summary:
At least one person killed and nearly 150,000 households lost electricity from North Carolina to New England

A strong, deadly storm known as a

blocks.text: A strong, deadly storm known as a nor’easter battered the US’s east coast over the weekend, bringing power outages, flooding, damaging winds and hazardous ocean conditions.

Trees and power lines were knocked down across the region, at least one person was killed and hundreds of thousands were left without electricity as officials cautioned that conditions could deteriorate further.

There was significant coastal flooding, rough surf, powerful winds, rain and dangerous rip currents from North Carolina through New England. Boston and the New York City tri-state area were among the regions affected.

blocks.caption: Waves crash over homes on Rebecca Road during a nor’easter on 26 September in Scituate, Massachusetts. Photograph: Scott Eisen/Getty Images

blocks.text: Power outages by Sunday were already widespread, with nearly 150,000 households losing electricity so far, according to the website Poweroutage.US.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) advised travelers to check with their airlines for updated flight information. FlightAware reported more than 3,000 US delays and nearly 430 cancellations.
As a result of the storm, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, declared a state of emergency covering the Bronx, Kings, Nassau, New York, Queens, Richmond, Suffolk and Westchester counties.

A fallen tree in the east New York City borough of Brooklyn resulted in a death on Saturday during the nor’easter. A 56-year-old New York City housing authority employee was killed when a tree came down on him in a parking lot.
Police said he was pronounced dead at Brookdale University hospital. Authorities had not immediately determined whether wind caused the tree to fall.

In Queens, high winds caused widespread disruption after a tree fell at about 5.40pm in the Glendale area, with downed power lines forcing authorities to close the roadway. As a precaution, the New York City fire department evacuated a nearby building. No injuries were reported in that incident.

blocks.caption: Crews work to clear fallen trees from the property of Burnet Hill’s Haunted Ridge after a nor’easter storm in Livingston, New Jersey, on Saturday. Photograph: Kyle Mazza/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Along the Jersey Shore, residents spent Saturday removing debris and cleaning up between periods of high tide after the nor’easter forced flood water into streets and homes near the New Jersey coast. Eight counties in New Jersey remain under a state of emergency issued before the coastal storm arrived.

The storm struck the mid-Atlantic and New England over the weekend and was forecast to continue into the early part of this week. As the week continues, flooding was expected to rise and recede along with the tides.

The National Weather Service (NWS) expected coastal flooding to bring significant flooding from the Jersey Shore south to the northern Outer Banks of North Carolina, with more moderate flooding forecast along the Massachusetts coast.

articles.title: Stronger maritime security eyed
articles.summary: At the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Saturday, the Philippines demanded stronger maritime security for Filipinos, who make up 25 percent of the world’s…

blocks.text: September 28, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — At the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Saturday, the Philippines demanded stronger maritime security for Filipinos, who make up 25 percent of the world’s seafarers.

Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said seafarers form an indispensable lifeline of global commerce, with nearly 90 percent of world trade moving by sea, supported by close to two million seafarers, adding that more than 25 percent of those seafarers are Filipinos.

“They are essential workers, yet increasingly vulnerable to conflict and attacks at sea,” Lazaro said, noting a recent incident in the Strait of Hormuz which claimed the lives of two Filipino seafarers and injured many others.
The two Filipino seafarers died following an attack in the Strait of Hormuz while aboard the M/V SIDR on Aug. 31.

“Their tragedy reminds us: Maritime security is human security. As an archipelagic and maritime nation, the Philippines cannot separate the safety of ships and seafarers from supply chains and global commerce,” Lazaro said.

She stressed that millions of migrant workers are entitled to full human rights and fundamental freedoms, regardless of status, and deserve steadfast protection from trafficking and exploitation along perilous migration routes.

“Open and secure seas, free from interference and coercion, are vital to our security, our economy and our people,” she said, emphasizing that international law, along with the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), must remain firmly as the constitution of the oceans.
Lazaro noted that 2027 marks the 45th anniversary of UNCLOS and the Manila Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of International Disputes.

articles.title: Venezuela releases dozens of political prisoners as election calls grow
articles.summary: A slew of dissidents being released from long-term detention comes days after the nation's interim leader met the US president.

blocks.text: Venezuelan authorities have released a slew of political prisoners, human rights groups say, days after the nation's interim leader met US President Donald Trump in New York.
Among those released in the early hours of Saturday morning was Wilder Vasquez, who was handed a five-year sentence in 2018 over claims he was plotting to kill former President Nicolás Maduro.
Opposition figures have renewed calls for free elections after interim President Delcy Rodriguez held talks with Trump, who captured Maduro earlier this year, at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.
Her administration previously released hundreds of prisoners as part of a reconciliation effort following Maduro's seizure.
However, these releases slowed to a trickle in April after Rodriguez said the scheme was "coming to an end".
Venezuela's government has not made any statement concerning the latest releases, nor has it indicated whether they were the result of her conversation with the US president.
Gonzalo Himiob, vice-president of rights group Foro Penal, said "a significant number" of political prisoners had been released on Saturday morning from several of Venezuela's detention centres.

Venezuelan Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, a minister closely associated with Maduro's authoritarian rule, called the interim president's meeting with Trump "a great triumph of the diplomacy of peace".
But opposition voices expressed their disapproval over the meeting, viewing it as a snub of their calls – that the US has previously endorsed – for swift elections.

Pedro Mario Burelli, a former Venezuelan state oil company executive and opposition commentator, called the two world leaders "the shameless puppet and her unscrupulous and undignified puppet-master", adding: "Little has changed in Venezuela under Washington's clumsy and selective oversight."

Venezuela's last elections, held in 2024, in which Maduro was declared the winner, were widely disputed as rigged. Opposition tallies suggested their candidate, who stood after Machado was barred from running, had won by 70% of the vote.

Despite this, the Trump administration backed Rodriguez, Maduro's former vice-president, as his successor rather than opposition leader María Corina Machado after Maduro was seized and put on trial on drug charges in January.
Analysts at the time cast this decision as the US choosing short-term stability in Venezuela until elections could be held.
Rodriguez used her UN General Assembly speech on Thursday to reiterate that there "will be elections in Venezuela", without specifying when.

articles.title: Two people killed as bus crashes on way to Oktoberfest
articles.summary: The bus was traveling from Italy to Munich, carrying 33 Filipino tourists who wanted to visit the famous beer festival. One of the dozens injured remains in life-threatening condition.

image.caption: Emergency services rushed to the scene of the crash in Buchloe, Bavaria near the Austrian border Image: Karl-Josef Hildenbrand/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two people were killed and many more injured when a bus carrying a group of Filipino tourists overturned in southern Germany on Sunday en route to the Munich Oktoberfest.
The bus was coming from Milan, an Italian city with a large Filipino community.

According to German police, there were 33 tourists on the bus when, at 5:41 a.m. local time (03:41 a.m. GMT), the vehicle went off the side of the A96 highway and overturned. No other vehicles were involved in the crash.

Six of the injured were immediately rushed by helicopter to nearby hospitals, one of whom was thought to still be in a life-threatening condition. Two more were taken by ambulance to the hospital, while another 22 were first treated at the scene before several of those were also brought to the hospital.
Police so far have only identified one of the two people who died as a 58-year-old Filipino citizen.

"It is naturally very chaotic at first, and establishing the facts is difficult,” explained a spokesperson for the local police headquarters. It took police hours to confirm how many people actually were on the bus.
Bus driver charged with negligent homicide

In addition to the 33 tourists, there were the two Italian bus drivers on board, both of whom were not injured in the crash. The driver who was at the wheel at the time of the crash is now being investigated for negligent homicide, police said. "That is standard procedure,” a police spokeswoman explained.

The cause of the accident remained unclear, police said. "The public prosecutor's office has commissioned an accident reconstruction expert report to determine the cause of the crash. It is far too early to comment.”

More than 200 firefighters, medics and police were rushed to the scene of the crash. A section of the highway was completely blocked for some time before, but in the afternoon, traffic was allowed to resume.
There have been a string of bus accidents in recent weeks. Earlier in September, a Dutch coach crashed in Switzerland, killing five, while a bus crash on Germany's A3 highway left 30 people injured.
Oktoberfest draws millions of visitors

Munich’s Oktoberfest is the world’s largest beer festival, attracting millions of visitors to the Bavarian capital each year. Held over roughly two weeks, it combines giant beer tents, traditional Bavarian food, live music and fairground rides, drawing visitors from Germany and around the world.

This year, the Oktoberfest runs from September 19 to October 4. Organizers said that at the halfway point, around 3.8 million people had already visited the festival — about 300,000 more than at the same point last year.

blocks.caption: The Oktoberfest is the world's biggest beer festival and draws millions of international touristsImage: Matthias Schrader/AP Photo/picture alliance

articles.title: Swiss voters reject stricter neutrality rules that would curb Nato cooperation
articles.summary:
70% vote against tightening centuries-old neutrality, which far right said was eroded by sanctions against Russia

Swiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal for a strict definition of…

blocks.text: Swiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal for a strict definition of neutrality that would have required Switzerland to curb cooperation with Nato and abandon sanctions against Russia.

All cantons and about 70% of voters rejected the proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be ⁠written into the Swiss constitution, final results from the Federal Statistical Office showed. The motion had been promoted by the far-right Swiss People’s party (SVP).
Although the defeat was expected, it will be a relief across Europe, amid increasing strains in maintaining EU unity on sanctions against Russia.

Switzerland’s centuries-old neutrality was formally recognised after the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815. Critics of current government policy claim that status has been eroded by Switzerland’s decision to mirror EU sanctions against Russia, after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Voters were asked to decide on enshrining the principle of “perpetual and armed neutrality” in the constitution and barring Switzerland from joining any military alliances or imposing sanctions on warring states, unless mandated by the United Nations.

The outcome is a heavy defeat for the SVP’s billionaire backer, Christoph Blocher, who was a prominent supporter of the initiative, reported by Bloomberg to have spent 2 million francs (€2.1m, £1.8m) on the campaign

Opponents welcomed the results. “Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on,” said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green party.

The Swiss government, along with most political parties, opposed the measure, arguing “Switzerland would cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy” leaving the country less secure in the event of an attack and heavily restricting its ability to cooperate with Nato.
Although not a member of Nato, Switzerland has cooperated with the transatlantic military alliance for 30 years.

Analysts said the result showed Swiss people were content with how the government interpreted Swiss neutrality. “The people have spoken: they accept that neutrality is an instrument that can evolve, leaving the government with room for manoeuvre to adapt its application faced with geopolitical upheavals,” wrote Katy Romy, a correspondent for SwissInfo, the online service of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation.
after newsletter promotion
She also wrote that the yes campaign was unable to shed perceptions it was acting in Russian interests.
Russia’s foreign ministry had praised the initiative, while criticising Switzerland’s adoption of EU sanctions and claiming the country was abandoning neutrality.
The SVP accepted the defeat and said it had no current plans for further action.

articles.title: Datacenter developers accused of skirting key US pollution rules
articles.summary:
Firms manipulating process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental groups warn

Datacenter developers are manipulating the EPA’s air pollution permitting…

blocks.text: Datacenter developers are manipulating the EPA’s air pollution permitting process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental advocates allege.

Companies need federal permits to emit a range of pollutants. In their permit applications, some in big tech are avoiding “major” reviews by dividing their emissions sources into separate, multiple “minor” sources that require less regulatory oversight, the advocates say.

This helps datacenters avoid public scrutiny, and permit applications are typically approved much faster. It also likely saves tech companies money, and avoids the hassle and cost of potential pollution controls, advocates say. Datacenters can be significant sources of nitrogen oxide, ozone, heavy metals, particulate matter, greenhouse gas and other dangerous air pollutants.

In North Carolina, Amazon and utility giant Duke Energy are installing 649 diesel generators to back up a new hyperscale center. They submitted two permits, and avoided a major review despite being in a low income area that already suffers from high levels of air pollution.

In New Mexico, the Project Jupiter datacenter developers attempted to circumvent a major review by proposing two natural gas “microgrids” for either side of the facility and submitting two “minor” permits. The overall project would have released enough pollution to trigger a major review.

In Frederick, Maryland, four datacenters with separate minor permits, including one by Amazon, operate on a single campus with a master developer, regulatory documents show. In other instances, data center developers have staggered minor permit requests over months that cumulatively emit as much pollution as a major source, advocates say.

These regulatory maneuvers make it less clear how much pollution residents living near the facilities are exposed to, and the move amounts to “lego permitting”, said Michael Koerber, a retired deputy director of the EPA’s Office of Air Quality Planning and Standards, which worked on permitting.

“They want to fly under the radar,” said Koerber, who now volunteers with the Environmental Protection Network nonprofit. “The more attention they have, the more difficult it gets to get the permit. They have consultants who are very good and know where the shortcuts are.”

Koerber noted that the situation is not unique to the data center industry. Cheryl Vetter, a former EPA employee who worked with Koeber and left the agency last year, said it was not common for data centers to use this tactic until after she left.
In a statement, an Amazon spokesperson said the company “appropriately applied for and obtained an air permit for our datacenter project”.

Under the Clean Air Act, companies building a project that will be a “major” source of air pollution, like some hyperscale data centers, are typically supposed to undergo a more stringent air emissions review. Among other protections, it is supposed to ensure that the pollution the facility would add to the local airshed would not violate air quality limits when combined with the air pollution already in the region.

This process can be lengthy, may require pre-construction monitoring, and, if the proposed data center is found to violate limits, may require companies to take steps to limit their pollution, like adding scrubbers to their smokestacks.

The Project Jupiter datacenter plans to divide its natural turbines into minor permits was “nothing short of preposterous”, attorneys with the New Mexico Environmental Law Center wrote in March comments submitted to state regulators. The firm is representing community members who would be impacted by the proposed plans’ pollution.

It in effect created a scenario in which one natural gas power plant would have operated with two minor permits, attorneys wrote. The permit application points to why the data center’s developers, Austin-based BorderPlex, attempted to do two permits.

The federal limit for a minor permit for hazardous air pollution is 25 tons per year. The project’s developers proposed releasing between 20.2 and 24.2 tons of hazardous air pollution from each of the grids, meaning that together they would have released as much as 44 tons of hazardous air pollution.

In regulatory documents, Maslyn Locke, an attorney working on the case, wrote that the “audacious attempt to arbitrarily distinguish two halves of the same source is insulting to both [regulators] and community members, as it is so clearly an attempt to avoid air pollution control requirements.”

The developer withdrew the application in April amid fierce community pushback, Locke said. The New Mexico environment department also opposed the proposal, a spokesperson told the Guardian. However, Locke told the Guardian there was no public evidence that regulators opposed it until now. New plans for the data center have been held up by the state supreme court over procedural problems, Locke said.

Vetter said the law allows for divided permits in some instances. Permits can be divided if two companies are polluting at the same location, but not if all the polluting activities are under common control. The sources must also be adjacent, though the definition of “adjacent” can include those that do not share a border, but operate as part of the same facility.

Amazon and Duke’s North Carolina plans call for nearly 250 tons per year of nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and volatile organic compounds. Amazon is proposing to emit about 98 tons of particulate matter annually, and 6.4 tons per year of hazardous air pollutants, including benzene and formaldehyde.

The heavily industrial region is already burdened by pollution from a Duke power plant and other plastic pellet factory, the Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC) wrote in comments to North Carolina state regulators.

Heart disease, cancer, and respiratory disease are among the leading causes of death in the region, and the datacenter’s diesel generators’ particulate matter and hazardous pollutants will almost certainly increase those problems, advocates warn.

It appears the companies split the permits to avoid a major review, Kathleen Sullivan, a SELC attorney, told the Guardian. North Carolina regulators wrote that Duke’s generators are providing temporary power for about a year, and that Duke is operating them separately from Amazon’s generators. But the companies did not provide to regulators lease agreements and contracts, and some documents suggest Amazon controls all the generators, Sullivan alleged.
In its statement, Amazon said: “The separate permitting of Amazon’s and Duke’s respective projects reflects the actual ownership and operational structure.”
“They should be – and are – permitted under separate air permits,” the spokesperson said.

Even if some of the generators are only temporary, high levels of exposure to the dangerous pollutants for even an hour can cause health problems, and the plans should undergo more meaningful scrutiny, Sullivan added.
She said state regulators are “simply trusting two extremely wealthy and politically powerful companies without any verification”.

“North Carolina regulators failed to protect people’s health and the air we all breathe by blindly accepting the companies’ self-interested statements instead of doing their job to investigate the key facts,” Sullivan said.

articles.title: European cities seek ways of boosting affordable housing
articles.summary: In many major urban centers of Europe, the housing shortage has become an explosive social issue. DW looks into various models that have been put in place across the continent.

image.caption: The Vienna model has provided affordable housing to Viennese residents for more than 100 years Image: DW

blocks.text: In the European Union's most populous city, pressure on the housing market is so great that many of its residents are willing to undertake a historic experiment: Five years ago, Berliners voted in a referendum to instruct the Senate of the German capital to draft a law that would put an end to the power of large real estate companies. Those that owned more than 3,000 units should be expropriated, they said. The Senate did not act on the results of the referendum, which was non-binding. Meanwhile, the average cost of new leases has since risen by about half.

But in the Berlin elections on September 20, the socialist Left Party, which in its campaign had promised to act on the referendum, won the largest share of the vote. Whether it will be able to make good on its promises now depends on how negotiations to form a coalition shape up. But whatever happens, the election has drawn attention once again to the severity of the housing crisis in many cities across Europe.

blocks.caption: Left Party candidate Elif Eralp has promised to be a mayor for all Berliners. Her campaign was largely about providing affordable housing. Image: Britta Pedersen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Here are some initiatives that have already been put in place:
Vienna: The city is the landlord

The Vienna model is a flagship solution to soaring rent prices in Europe. The ambitious social housing program as introduced after World War I when the Austrian capital experienced a severe housing crisis. Beds were so scarce that some workers had to sleep in shifts. Diseases such as tuberculosis spread in the cramped living conditions.

The model serves to stabilize the city's housing market to this day: According to the Vienna authorities, the city owns approximately 220,000 municipal apartments that it rents out as well as 200,000 subsidized dwellings. More than 60% of Vienna's residents live in one of these two types of housing. This also helps to stabilize prices on the private market.
Public funds in Vienna keep rents down
Basel: Public land, private buildings

The fact that housing is becoming increasingly expensive in many cities is largely due to the fact that a city's attractiveness is reflected in land prices. In many places, people are considering how to decouple rents from the price of land. One means of doing this is not to sell municipal land but to lease it to cooperatives or socially-conscious investors. This benefits councils that do not have to bear construction costs and developers too, as they do not have to factor in exorbitant land costs that are ultimately passed on to tenants.

The Swiss city of Basel is one of the pioneers of this model. About 40% of all cooperative housing units are located on public land. The Spanish city of Barcelona and the Portuguese capital Lisbon have also stepped up efforts to put this model in place.
Paris: Buying back office buildings and converting them into homes

It is harder if land and buildings are in private hands. In 2014, the French capital Paris launched an anti-displacement plan giving the municipality a "first right of refusal" in gentrifying neighborhoods to increase the share of affordable housing in the city. The current target is 30% social housing for low-income residents by 2035

Earlier this year, the French government and the Paris regional authorities identified 61 projects that could convert empty office buildings into housing and create up to 8,200 homes in the inner suburbs of the French capital.

blocks.caption: Certain office buildings in the Paris suburbs are being converted into affordable homes Image: Vincent Isore/IP3press/imago images

blocks.text: Prague: Apartments for public-sector workers

The Czech capital has found another way to keep those without whom the city could not function in Prague: caregivers, police officers, teachers and sanitation workers. Some 660 new energy-efficient apartments reserved specifically for public-sector employees have just been built.

The subsidiary of a Czech bank, which has received European loans, handled the development. The aim is to keep rents 20% below the market rate thanks to economies of scale, and it is not the bank who decides on the tenants but hospitals or public sector agencies, which draw up leases and can attract new employees with affordable rent options. More apartments are currently being planned.

blocks.caption: Few people can afford to live in the center of PragueImage: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: Dublin: Non-profit cost rental housing

It has also become difficult for people with low incomes to stay in the Irish capital Dublin. During and after Ireland's financial crisis of 2008, foreign investors bought up a lot of real estate and at the same time rents skyrocketed when several major tech companies chose Dublin as their EU headquarters because of favorable tax rates. There are now long waiting lists for public housing in the city whose supply remains too low.

In 2021, the Irish government introduced the Cost Rental Housing program to provide housing to those on middle incomes, i.e. those who earn too much to qualify for public housing but too little to have a chance on the private market. To qualify in Dublin, a household has to have a net income of below €66,000 ($75,000) per year. Non-profits or public agencies lease out the apartments and rents are below market levels, by an average of almost 30% according to a recent study by the Dublin-based Economic & Social Research Institute (ESRI).

The Irish government hopes to be able to deliver 18,000 low-cost rental homes by the end of the decade. Last year, there were more than 4,200 applicants for 104 apartments in a new community in a suburb of Dublin.
This article was translated from German.
Berlin has space, so why is housing so expensive?

articles.title: UK: 5 arrested after 'major incident' near Fairford air base
articles.summary: Scores of homes were evacuated in the UK town of Whelford, near an air base used by the US military, with bomb disposal teams checking "suspicious vehicles" at the scene. Police said five men had…

image.caption: The US Air Force has used the British base for attacks against IranImage: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: British authorities evacuated buildings and deployed military bomb disposal teams over a "major incident" in the town of Whelford on Sunday morning.
The town is located near the Fairford air base, which is used by the US military. Around 30 emergency vehicles were seen in the area, including police cars, ambulances, and fire engines.
Counter-terrorism police were leading the investigation. On Sunday afternoon, London's Metropolitan police said five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a "terrorist act."

blocks.caption: UK police blocked roads leading to the Fairford air baseImage: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: Previously, the authorities said that several men were "arrested on suspicion of offences the ​Explosives Act."
"A cordon is currently in place but we'd like to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained," British police said.
Bomb disposal units examining three 'suspicious vehicles'
Separately, local police said they had received a call earlier on Sunday about "three suspicious vehicles" heading to the base.
"Armed officers responded and subsequently arrested five men in the Whelford area," assistant chief constable Richard Ocone told reporters.
He added that a cordon of 400 meters, or approximately 1/4 of a mile, has been put in place around the vehicles "while the army's explosive ordinance disposal unit examine them."
"As a precaution, around 85 households have been advised to evacuate while these examinations take place," Ocone said.
He added that some of the evacuees were taken to a nearby leisure center.
The Gloucestershire police representative also asked the public "not to speculate" but follow official channels instead.
Officials stay tight-lipped

A spokesperson for ​the US Air Force refused to discuss specific steps when contacted by the Reuters news agency, saying only that both US and British forces "remain vigilant and will take ⁠appropriate ​actions to ensure the safety and security of our ​US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families."

blocks.caption: This Fairford base gates was blocked by construction machinery Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: The background for the incident was not immediately clear.

The UK has allowed the US to use Fairford for its war against Iran, with Iran's Revolutionary Guards warning UK officials against the move this summer.
